author: Naguib Mahfouz
introFa: کتاب «Children of Gebelawi» نوشته Naguib Mahfouz یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Children of Gebelawi»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: 117 M’ CHILDREN OF GEBELAWI Blackwell Publishing Ltd Oxford, UK MUWO The Muslim World 06105-2260 © 2002 Hartford Seminary January 2003 93 1000 Original Article The Muslim World • Volume 93 • January 2003 Mahfouz’s Chicdaen of Sebecawi Gender in an Allegorical Life of Muhammad: Mahfouz’s Children of Gebelawi Ruth Roded Hebrew University Jerusalem, Israel He was much moved by her gentleness and affection, as he was whenever he was lucky enough to meet her. It was an affection of a kind he had never known except from what he had heard about mother-love. If his mother had lived she would have been about this woman’s age, about forty. How wonderful this quality seemed in an alley that took pride in strength and violence. The only thing more wonderful was her shy beauty and the joy it breathed into him. It was not like the hot-blooded adventures in the desert with their blind, burning hunger and their sad, transient satisfaction.1 T he psychological insight which the Egyptian author Naguib Mahfouz brings to the description of the love, which the character he has created based on Muhammad’s life feels for his ﬁrst wife, bears the imprint of a great thinker and an original writer. Orphaned as an infant, deprived of a mother’s love, he was naturally drawn to a mother ﬁgure in the shape of a woman twenty years his senior. The above quotation also addresses two themes prevalent in many modern biographies of the Prophet — violence and sensuality. Mahfouz’s Muhammad appreciates gentleness in a world dominated by violence, and values the joy of mature love after having experienced the shallow, yet intense passion of youthful sexuality. The biography of the Prophet is a dramatic narrative that has gripped the imagination of Muslims of all walks of life for over fourteen hundred years. The most familiar classical life of Muhammad, the earliest extant biography of the Prophet, was composed by Ibn Ishaq and has survived in the edited version of Ibn Hisham. The work has been a prominent part of the Islamic

T M W• V 93 • J 2003 118 scholarly canon through the centuries and to this day. Parallel to these Islamic developments but to a great extent independent of them, the life of Muhammad became a central theme in the Christian polemic against Islam from the Middle Ages, with gender issues a major component of these attacks. From the mid-nineteenth century and throughout the twentieth, Muslims in various parts of the world began to compose modern biographies of the Prophet. Apparently, the ﬁrst modern Muslim biography of the Prophet was a series of essays composed by the great Indian reformer Sir Sayyid Ahmad Khan in 1870, in response to William Muir’s four-volume Life of Muhammad from Original Sources.2 More inﬂuential was the work of the Indian Amir ‘Ali which was eventually published under the title The Spirit of Islam.3 The book was immensely popular in the West where nine English editions were produced between 1922 and 1961, and also impressed Western educated Muslims from the Indian subcontinent to Egypt.4 From the 1930s, virtually every major literary ﬁgure in Egypt composed a modern biography of the Prophet. Muhammad Husayn Haykal began publishing a series of articles in 1932 reviewing a French life of Muhammad.5 The articles eventually evolved into one of the most popular and inﬂuential modern Muslim biographies of the Prophet.6 Among other Egyptian life stories of Muhammad were: Taha Husayn’s “Ala al-hamish al-sira (On the Margin of the Sira) (1933–1943); Tawfiq al-Hakim’s play Muhammad: Al-Rasul Al- Bashar (Muhammad: The Human Prophet) published in 1936; ‘Abbas Mahmud al-‘Aqqad’s ‘Abqariyyat Muhammad (The Genius of Muhammad ) (1942); and Fa†hi Radwan’s Al-Tha’ir al-A“zam (The Greatest Revolutionary) (1954).7 Naguib Mahfouz’s version of the life of Muhammad was even more revolutionary than those of his predecessors in that it was translated into literary ﬁction. Mahfouz’s allegorical rendition of the life of Muhammad — ﬁrst published in 1959 — was produced against the background of sweeping changes in the lives of Egyptian men and women. The author’s life experience, spent almost exclusively in Cairo, primed him to document and critique the social realities of his time. Mahfouz has gone to great lengths to obscure and even disguise his family life, yet gender analysis of his early works reveals a blend of feminism and humanistic realism. In his stories of the prophets and tale of the life of Muhammad, Mahfouz takes his unique blend of spirituality and humanism to a new plane. Naguib Mahfouz’s allegorical life of Muhammad immediately aroused opposition among Egypt’s religious establishments but it eventually contributed to the worldwide recognition of his literature. As his fame grew, Islamists joined the chorus of those who regarded Mahfouz’s work as

M’ CHILDREN OF GEBELAWI 119 blasphemy. They were incapable of understanding that the novelist regarded the biography of the Prophet as a source of inspiration and imagery for the arts. The Historical–Cultural Backdrop Naguib Mahfouz (b. 1911) is the quintessential Egyptian, rarely having left his homeland, and to a great extent a product of its history and culture. Historical developments in Egypt up to the time he ﬁrst published his work on Muhammad (1959) clearly informed his early work. After World War I, competing political ideologies — liberalism, socialism and communism, neo-Islamism, and fascism — vied for the allegiance of Egyptians and for dominance in the political arena. The 1952 coup of the Free Ofﬁcers promised energetic, new solutions to Egypt’s problems, and a revolutionary platform gradually evolved.8 In the inter-war period, Egypt had undergone socio-economic transformations with dire consequences for the common people. City-dwellers experienced a multiplicity of changes in their traditional, daily lifestyles, and adopted the trappings and sometimes values of “modernity” and “Westernization.”9 Mahfouz, the consummate Cairene, lived these transformations. The 1952 revolution proved a disappointment to many intellectuals in its failure to signiﬁcantly improve the lot of the common people and its use of force to suppress dissenting voices.10 Mahfouz’s gender perception was informed by an Egyptian feminism that traced its origins to the nineteenth century, and the introduction of a number of modest but symbolically important innovations in some women’s lives. State schools for girls were established, women’s journals appeared, calls for the liberation of women emerged from various circles, and public lectures by and for women were introduced. Women’s philanthropic organizations were formed in Egypt as early as 1908, and the ﬁrst women’s political and feminist organizations were established as an outcome of the national revolution of 1919. During the 1920s, a number of laws were passed that reformed family law by codifying select readings of Islamic law. Women’s call for the vote, however, was denied from the onset of parliamentary life in the early 1920’s, despite their part in the national struggle.11 From the 1930s, the feminist movement gradually expanded from a small coterie of upper-class women to broader social and geographic circles. A signiﬁcant achievement occurred in the elections of 1957 when Egyptian women voted for the ﬁrst time, and two women entered the parliament in one- party elections under the aegis of ‘Abd al-Nasir’s National Union.12 Women were also active in the full range of ideological movements that functioned in Egypt at this time. As early as 1936, Zaynab al-Ghazali (1918–) founded the Muslim Women’s Association, and a small number of women were involved in

T M W• V 93 • J 2003 120 the Egyptian Communist Party. ‘Abd al-Nasir’s policy of political and social mobilization naturally lead to the adoption of state feminism whereby the government advocated improving women’s situation but also co-opted independent women’s associations under the aegis of the ministry for social affairs.13 In short, during the early years of Naguib Mahfouz’s literary endeavors, the issue of women’s rights continued to be on Egyptian intellectuals’ agenda. No less important, economic and social changes impacted the lives of women of all classes — for better and for worse. Mahfouz selected literary expression as his life’s work at a time when there was a tremendous cultural outpouring in Egypt characterized by innovations in genres and style. Many of the short stories, novels, dramas, and ﬁlms dealt with political and socio-economic problems Egypt faced. Intermittent censorship and self-censorship plagued writers of the period. The Nasirist policy of mobilization of the arts for the government’s purposes certainly lead to even greater censorship. On the other hand, certain works could be published under the aegis of the centralist Nasirist regime that might have raised a popular outcry in the pre-revolutionary years. Naguib Mahfouz was at the center of these exciting developments in Egyptian intellectual and cultural life. The novel was considered a uniquely European genre with tenuous prose antecedents in classical Arabic literature. Early Arabic novels were produced in Egypt from the end of the nineteenth century. They were didactic, historical romances, harking back to chapters in Egyptian history but also aiming at current political affairs. The ﬁrst indigenous, realistic novel Zaynab, published by Haykal in 1913, is the melodramatic story of a peasant girl. In the 1930s, many Egyptian literati tried their hand at this genre, and after these early attempts, around the year 1939, a generation of novelists emerged producing more mature work. Of this group, Naguib Mahfouz was to take the Arabic novel to unprecedented heights.14 The Life of the Writer Mahfouz was born in 1911 and spent the formative years of his life in the old quarter of Jamaliyya in Cairo, a world that was to become a microcosm of civilized society in his literary works.15 In “Mahfouzland,” as Enany has termed the semi-realistic, semi-symbolic world which the writer created in his work,16 the primordial wasteland (khala” ) became a wild refuge, beyond the pale of civilization, but also an ideal setting for spiritual meditation. Mahfouz attended a traditional Qur’anic school before studying at state primary and secondary schools. He became an avid reader at an early age, reading, among others, the works of Taha Husayn, ‘Abbas Mahmud al-‘Aqqad, Muhammad Husayn Haykal, and (at a slightly later stage) Tawfiq al-Hakim.17

M’ CHILDREN OF GEBELAWI 121 The greatest inﬂuence on his intellectual development, by his own testament, was Taha Husayn’s famous book Fi al-shi“r al-jahili (On Pre-Islamic Poetry) (1926), which questioned the authenticity of this literature and the received wisdom on the origin of Islam. In Mahfouz’s view, this book “elevated reason, giving it priority above tradition.”18 As a university student, Mahfouz studied philosophy and published a number of articles in magazines and newspapers dealing with philosophical and psychological subjects.19 When he decided to devote himself to literature rather than philosophy, he embarked on a self-styled program of reading world literature, primarily in English, to a much lesser extent in French, and in Arabic translation, where these were available.20 At the same time, Mahfouz started a life-long job as a government employee. This career choice would appear strange for a writer with original ideas since the threat of dismissal would constantly be hanging over his head if his writings aroused ire in government circles or among the public. In fact, none of Mahfouz’ work seem to have provoked reactions of this type until the publication of his religious allegory in 1959. This does not mean that he did not express unpopular ideas, but he was careful and sophisticated enough to do so in an encrypted way. Moreover, his works are quite complex, embodying a multiplicity of messages (as we shall see). From the early 1950s until his retirement in 1971, he held a number of fairly inﬂuential positions in the government’s newly formed administration of information and culture. ‘Abd al-Nasir’s revolutionary regime that evolved in Egypt after 1952 recognized the importance of these ﬁelds to disseminate its message and mobilize the population, and therefore, expanded and nationalized them.21 These credentials and personal connections undoubtedly stood him in good stead when he published Awlad Haratina as a series of stories in al-Ahram, the popular daily edited by Muhammad Hasanayn Haykal, a personal friend of ‘Abd al-Nasir’s. Mahfouz has been reticent about his private life, and he has frequently disseminated disinformation on his family not only to the public but to friends and relatives as well. His father, ‘Abd al-‘Aziz, a government ofﬁcial who became a store accountant, died in 1937. Mahfouz has never, however, used his father’s name as a surname, as it is common in Egypt. Little is known about his mother, not even her name. Naguib Mahfouz was the youngest of seven children, and for some time supported his mother and widowed sister. He remained a bachelor until the age of 43 during which time, however, he had many liaisons with women. In 1954, he married — not to one of the reasonable matches his mother urged on him, but rather to a woman he met through a friend. He was to recall, twenty-ﬁve years later, his fear at going against his mother’s wishes and his reluctance to tell her of his marriage.

T M W• V 93 • J 2003 122 Mahfouz has two daughters. He describes himself as a devoted family man, but also emphasizes his wife’s understanding and support.22 Prelude to Muhammad: Mahfouz’s Early Works Mahfouz, like many other aspiring young writers, began his literary career by publishing short stories in the Egyptian press and journals. These short stories are not considered of high literary quality, but they presage many of the themes that Mahfouz would deal with in his future work: unrequited love for a supercilious woman, the stern yet absent mother and the indulgent mother, corruption in government circles, the appeal of religious preachers to the common people and their concomitant threat to the authorities.23 Mahfouz’s earliest novels were three stories of a planned series of forty historical works set in ancient Egypt (published 1939–1944). The historical setting, however, thinly veiled a concern with contemporary social and political issues such as the Egyptians’ struggle against foreign domination and the ruler’s power conﬂict with the religious elite.24 After World War II, Mahfouz abandoned the Pharoanic metaphor for a series of realistic novels dealing directly with the suffering of the men and women of Cairo before and during the war.25 Of these, al-Sarab (The Mirage), has remained one of his most popular novels, running to thirteen printings by 1987. The story tells of a young man who was raised by an over-indulgent mother and is unable to have normal relations with women. Eventually, he establishes a relationship with a widow in her forties. Apparently, it is Mahfouz’s exposé of the repressive and hypocritical attitude to sex that accounts for the novel’s popularity.26 At the same time, he ventured into the world of cinema. From the late 1940s and through the 1950s, Mahfouz made a major contribution to the emergence of the wave of Egyptian realist ﬁlms.27 In the mid-1950s, Mahfouz published the trilogy devoted to the saga of one middle-class Cairo family during the period between the world wars.28 Most critics were impressed with the painstaking reconstruction of the physical and social milieu of an old quarter of Cairo in bygone days. The tension between tradition and modernity undoubtedly infuses this, as it does other works by Mahfouz, although the author’s attitude to this dichotomy is far more complex than some critics have led us to believe. The trilogy contains much anecdotal information about culture-speciﬁc gender-related customs and attitudes, but this opus magnum seems to be about profound human relations within the family and in interaction with the surrounding society that transcend the cultural context of Cairo between the wars. Gender in the early works of Mahfouz and, in particular, his massive trilogy, is a subject worthy of separate study.29 Mahfouz depicted a large number of women in a wide variety of situations deriving in part from their

M’ CHILDREN OF GEBELAWI 123 ages, cohorts, social strata and economic classes. The roles of women in society as portrayed in these novels changes over time, and individual women evolve in the course of their lifetimes. Are these changes completely for the better? The answer does not seem to be clear-cut.30 The mother ﬁgure dominates these works. “Dominates” seems an inappropriate term because the mother appears to be dominated by a classic, almost caricatured, patriarchal society, but in fact she often takes command of the family. The widowed mother in Bidaya wa-nihaya (The Beginning and the End ) leads the family with wisdom and ﬁrmness, despite three grown-up sons who regard her as omnipotent. She had made family decisions, we learn, even before the father’s death. In Midaq Alley (Zuqaq al-Midaq), a mother considers her adult son and his father as stupid and does not take them seriously. The matriarch in the trilogy has a strong impact on the family, she is aware of events outside the home and views them from her own perspective, and as the father weakens and dies, her role grows.31 Milson’s thought-provoking thesis of the “absent father” and the “persevering mother” in Mahfouz’ early realistic novels leads him to conclude that the author views women in a more sympathetic light than he sees men.32 The image of women beating their husbands appears repeatedly in Midaq Alley, and is even referred to in Bidaya wa-nihaya.33 In the context of Mahfouz’s realistic novels, the female “husband-beater” deﬁes common wisdom about exclusively male family violence in patriarchal, Middle Eastern societies. Although folk-tales about a husband being beaten by his wife have been recorded, it is frequently assumed that this is mere hyperbole for the amusement of the listeners.34 Mahfouz’s description of wives berating their husbands in public, albeit in a ﬁctional setting, points to an aspect of gendered social reality that has eluded the eye of the historian. Human sexuality is recognized as an integral part of life but romantic love is also depicted. Female singers and prostitutes are strong, proud, even haughty ﬁgures compared to the seemingly cowed family women. Based on an analysis of the prostitutes in Mahfouz’ work as rebels against traditional social expectations, Miriam Cooke concludes that in his early work of the 1940s and 50s, he “may be dubbed a feminist.”35 The idealized object of romantic love can also be a rather cruel temptress. A young barber’s blind love for an aloof, unkindly and even contemptuous young woman in Midaq Alley; the young student’s distant infatuation ﬁrst for a neighbor and later for a pasha’s daughter; and Kamel’s adolescent romantic ardor for a clearly unattainable, upper-class young lady who seems to be ﬂirting with him all appear tragi-comic.36 These episodes demonstrate the power that the idealized image of chaste, young women may have over vulnerable young men. This

T M W• V 93 • J 2003 124 power is enhanced by the physical and social distance between men and women that ampliﬁes male fantasies, prompting them to construct women’s thoughts in their imaginations rather than reach out to women’s real feelings and aspirations. It is typical of Mahfouz, that these strong women exist in a world in which a young woman who leaves the conﬁnes of her small alley inevitably becomes a prostitute; a father forbids his daughter to continue her education despite the economic advantages; and a woman of the older generation may not leave her home without her husband’s permission, even to visit a holy shrine.37 Moreover, proper women eventually succumb to arranged marriages no matter how liberal they may have seemed and what machinations they may have had to employ. In a sign of the times, Mahfouz also introduced women in relatively new roles such as factory women, whose morals, like those of their European counterparts, are suspect. A female journalist, for instance, is not only a career woman but a leftist to boot.38 He notes that women’s education can lead to income-producing endeavors such as teaching, and that women with a profession have greater independence and can even forgo marriage.39 A clinging dress, revealing a young woman’s arms, the lower part of her legs and her neck is considered decent and almost prudish.40 Mahfouz’s early works were infused with Islamic terminology, had ambivalent religious characters and contained Muslim metaphors even for profane objects and acts. In the last volume of the trilogy, published shortly before Awlad Haratina, Mahfouz hints at one of the major themes of his next work — the scientist as prophet of the modern world, “Science must take the place that prophecy and religion had in the ancient world,” the editor of al- Insan al-Jadid/The New Man tells his young protégé. “Be as zealous about [modern science] as if you were religious and remember that each age has its prophets. The prophets of this era are the scientists.”41 At the very end of the saga, however, it is the ancient shaykh who survives the deaths of so many family members, mocked by some of the younger generation but fondly regarded by Mahfouz’ alter ego, Kamal.42 Stories of the Prophets In Awlad Haratina, literally “Children of Our Quarter” but translated as Children of Gebelawi, the scope has been widened from a family or neighborhood to human society’s struggle for social justice. The relationship between man and God in this endeavor is explored, and an attempt is made to fathom God’s role in the development of human civilization.43 In this respect, as in others, it is reminiscent of John Steinbeck’s East of Eden (1952). Ordinary humans cannot comprehend the apparent indifference of the Creator

M’ CHILDREN OF GEBELAWI 125 to their suffering and weave miraculous legends around the deeds of messengers who try to ameliorate their lives.44 The framework of Mahfouz’s work is similar to a world history in Islamic tradition (like that of Tabari and others), dealing with events from Adam and Eve’s expulsion from the Garden of Eden up to the lifetime of the author. It is also similar to the stories of the prophets of Qisa’i and Tha‘alabi, comprising a series of biographies of Adam (Adham), Moses (Gebel, mountain), Jesus (Rifaa), Kassem (Muhammad) and Arafa (modern science). Each of the prophet’s attempts to redress the economic and social injustices of the neighborhood society, and each fails, including the modern scientist. Much has been made of the fact that the founder of the neighborhood, the forefather of all its residents, Gebelawi, is apparently killed at the end of the book by Arafa. The chapter devoted to Kassem=Muhammad is the longest in the book. Although an allegory and work of ﬁction, there is no question that this is Mahfouz’s reading of the life of the Prophet Muhammad. For one thing, unlike Salman Rushdie, who has publicly and repeatedly denied that his Satanic Verses depicts the Prophet of Islam, Naguib Mahfouz has not done so. Moreover, a host of details are drawn from traditional Islamic biographies of the Prophet. The fascinating aspect of this depiction of Muhammad, however, is precisely Mahfouz’s literary interpretation. What is unique about Mahfouz’s Muhammad? Certainly, the gender issue is a major theme in the chapter both quantitatively and qualitatively. But it would seem that Kassem=Muhammad differs from the previous prophets by merging their messages of the use of force and mercy when he says: “Damn all chiefs; there’s no peace and no safety where they are. We shall raise our cudgels as Gebel did, but for the sake of the mercy that Rifaa called for. Then we’ll use the estate for the common good to realize Adham’s dream; that’s our task, not being chiefs.”45 From the outset, Kassem=Muhammad opposes violence and teaches that “wisdom is better than force.”46 Nevertheless, a sports club is the metaphor for the social framework he establishes to attract young men and train them in body and mind for the “team.” At ﬁrst, the violence in the sports club seems like fun and games but later its darker side is revealed when it is used for serious purposes.47 Youth movements of this type were socio-political adjuncts of various right and left wing ideological movements in Egypt (as in many parts of the world) during the 1930s and 40s. Their seemingly recreational activities did in fact evolve into violent street ﬁghts over political power. Kassem=Muhammad’s aim, however, is not to rule the neighborhood.48 Only reluctantly does he resort to ﬁghting, and prefers cunning to strength.49 But violence is a part of human nature and when used by the enemy, must be returned in kind.

T M W• V 93 • J 2003 126 The struggle to bring social justice to the quarter is Kassem=Muhammad’s main objective, just as it was for the prophets that preceded him, and he achieves unprecedented brotherhood, love and peace.50 But this illusory achievement seems unreal in the harsh light of current social reality, apparently undermined by the disunity, ambition, and bloodshed of Kassem=Muhammad’s followers. The Muslims rule but their society is fraught with poverty and despair, and the dreams of the drugged storytellers.51 Mahfouz obliquely relates to a few miracles associated with the life of Muhammad.52 The author’s view that miracles are the opiate of the downtrodden is subtly but ﬁrmly conveyed in the summation and transition sections of the life of each prophet. Miracles also seem to fulﬁll individual psychological needs, as when Kassem=Muhammad believes he has seen the Angel in his hour of need. Most important, the Prophet truly believes that he has been chosen by divine intervention to liberate the people (as have the prophets before him), and struggles to recruit followers to his mission. The most fundamental article of faith — the revelation to Muhammad of a new message, more perfect than those received by previous prophets — is never overtly denied. Interfaith relations are not a major theme in Mahfouz’s life of Muhammad and do not depart much from views expressed in classical Muslim texts. Kassem=Muhammad follows in the tradition of his predecessors, Moses and Jesus, and is superior to them.53 The Jews are proud, even supercilious, provoking the animosity of others.54 The Jews and Christians ﬁght among themselves, and the Christians express hatred for Jews as well as the Muslims.55 After Kassem=Muhammad’s victory, he preaches to a mixed audience of Muslims, Christians and Jews. There were a few Jews and some Christians, however, who whispered concealed feelings of resentment at being ruled by a Muslim. But some Muslims had in fact become haughty.56 A hint of the Arab nationalism that was a rising ideology of collective identity in Egypt from the 1930s and to a greater extent in the late 1950s may be found in a meeting of Kassem=Muhammad with a very old woman, “mother of us all.”57 She tells him that the Arabs (Jerboas) hardly knew themselves and would never have become prominent were it not for him. This anecdote of the mother of the nation dovetails with the view that among the Prophet Muhammad’s many accomplishments was the creation of a nation out of the divided tribes of Arabia. Gender Relations in an Idealized Cairo Quarter Mahfouz’s broad approach to gender relations in Awlad Haratina is to portray them realistically but to depict women favorably on the whole, particularly Muslim women. When Kassem enters a private courtyard, for

M’ CHILDREN OF GEBELAWI 127 example, he calls out “Veils on!” a warning to the women of the household that a strange man was entering their domain.58 Mature women of all ages wear wraps and veils whenever they leave the house.59 These customs were apparently still prevalent in Mahfouz’s time in line with the strict rules of female seclusion he portrays among certain social groups in his other works. Moreover, woman is a metaphor for a variety of negative qualities, ranging from simplicity and cunning to weakness and cowardice.60 Although Mahfouz is cognizant of the patriarchal aspects of society, he also projects a feminist message. The Prophet’s sexuality is not denied but he also achieves an idealized monogamous, domestic life. As a young man, Kassem=Muhammad is “crazy about women,” unlike the Jesus ﬁgure.61 The sexual instinct, in Mahfouz’s view, may defy rationality, but sexuality like aggression is an innate human quality.62 His physical attraction to his second wife, a lovely girl of twelve or so, is mentioned repeatedly.63 Mahfouz ﬁnds a sensible and human explanation for the Prophet’s relationship with the child-bride ‘A’isha, so criticized by non-Muslims and apologetically defended by Muslims. The twelve-year-old actually looked older than her age, and we imagine a Lolita-like pre-adolescent rather than a child playing with dolls (as in the early Islamic sources). The Prophet’s subsequent marriages are clearly shown as the outcome of his attraction to beautiful women.64 Although his polygamous marriages are only brieﬂy referred to, this seems to be a structural decision, since there is no attempt to occult the Prophet’s numerous wives and give an impression of monogamy, as some Muslim authors of modern siras have chosen to do. The classic explanation for the Prophet’s multiple marriages, that they were to cement socio-political alliances, is raised. But Mahfouz emphasizes that in this social milieu, no explanation or justiﬁcation is required, for men are greatly admired for their virility and love of women. Moreover, Mahfouz presents a unique psychological insight into the Prophet’s numerous marriages—his incessant search for the love he had enjoyed and lost with his ﬁrst wife. The Prophet’s ﬁrst wife Khadija, named here Kamar or moon, a traditional Middle Eastern symbol of beauty, dominates the chapter devoted to the life of Muhammad. Her relationship with Muhammad, a relatively short episode in the early Islamic sources, comprises more than half of the chapter, and even after her death, she is an integral part of the action, up to the very end.65 Mrs. Kamar, a wealthy widow, was the only woman among the Arabs who owned property. Despite Mahfouz’s clear feminist message, he does not fall into the classic trap of regarding this unique woman as a sign that female merchants were prevalent among the Arabs, as many others have done. Kassem=Muhammad is immediately attracted to her ﬁne qualities—her tenderness and kindness—as well as her beauty.66 He is not interested in her

T M W• V 93 • J 2003 128 money or exploiting her love for him, but rather expresses love, consideration, compassion and longing for her throughout his life, even after her death and his marriage to other women.67 She is physically attractive, “beautifully plump, soft and sweet” but demure, and her support and consideration for him make her the perfect wife for the kind of companionate marriage that had become ideal among middle and upper-class Egyptian women and men since the nineteenth century.68 One is tempted to regard the character of Kamar as one more of Mahfouz’s strong mother ﬁgures, but one who in an idealized family is loved and appreciated by the man in her life. Kamar is also an active participant in the public sphere along with men, and her essential role in her husband’s mission is even expanded in comparison to classical sources. Strangely, after her death, Kamar=Khadija’s voice is linked to a vision of Kindil=Jibril just before Kassem=Muhammad’s ﬁrst battle.69 It is as if she has become his guardian angel in death as she was his support in life. The reality of gender relations in the world Mahfouz has crafted is of patriarchy, exploitation and objectiﬁcation of women, as in his earlier novels. Following many Muslim depictions of the improvement of the status of women with the advent of Islam, Kassem=Muhammad’s message contains an explicit call for women’s economic rights. Similarly, in accordance with classical sources often highlighted by modern feminists and liberals, both women and men are among his followers. Mahfouz’s personal critique of patriarchal society seems to be reﬂected in Kassem’s tender love for his only daughter that embodies no sign of his longing for a son or regret that he has no male offspring.70 Mahfouz’s attitude toward women’s belligerency is expressed, as in the foundation text, in the story of the battle of Uhud, but there are a number of interesting reversals in his version. From the onset, it is the men among Kassem’s opponents rather than the women who express the wish for vengeance in the most vicious terms. We are told that the wife of the Trustee objected to killing Kassem, whereas in the classical sources, Hind bt. ’Utba, wife of the leader of the pagans, is the epitome of unbridled revenge. Similarly, it is the enemy men who hurl curses and insults at Kassem’s followers, rather than the pagan Meccan women whose verbal assaults have become famous. Moreover, it is the enemy chief who twice threatens to proscribe a decent burial for Kassem’s ﬁghters, not the women who were charged in pre-Islamic tribal warfare and in this battle in particular with mutilating the bodies of the fallen enemy. Another male leader of Kassem’s antagonists speaks of drinking his blood, seemingly a reversal of Hind’s vile act of eating Hamza’s liver. Finally, Kassem himself leads the men in dragging the body of his archenemy and throwing it at the feet of the attackers, earning them the epithet

M’ CHILDREN OF GEBELAWI 129 “monsters.” Nevertheless, this act is described as necessary to save his people, rather than the despicable revenge attributed to Hind.71 Gendered roles in warfare are not that clear-cut in this battle constructed by Mahfouz, at least in part because of the ecological setting of the ﬁghting in a neighborhood quarter. On the one hand, women are more fearful than men and must be protected if possible. Their involvement seems to be limited to auxiliary functions such as preparing food, transmitting warnings and dressing wounds. On the other hand, the women want to participate in the ﬁghting, are ordered to join the guards and actually defend the path against the attackers. For the most part, both men and women throw stones at the attackers as would be expected in urban ﬁghting, but gendered differentiation of weapons is referred to when the men bring their cudgels and women baskets of stones. The ambivalence toward the participation of women in the battle is expressed when the enemy cries out: “Come down if you’re men! Come down you women, you bastards.”72 This ironical taunt can be interpreted as an insult to Kassem’s male ﬁghters who are no better than women and as a slur for their use of women in battle. At one point, as we have seen, Kassem meets a very old woman, so old that she saw Rifaa when she was young.73 This old woman, referred to as “mother of us all” is not only a link to the past but a source of ancient knowledge and wisdom. After the defeat of Kassem’s enemies in battle, a number of outspoken women challenge the chief and deny his lame excuses, but the establishment tries to shut them up.74 Women’s knowledge, understanding and words may be powerful and even dangerous. Opposition of the Religious Establishments and Worldwide Acclaim As soon as the ﬁrst chapters of Awlad Haratina appeared in al-Ahram, religious authorities condemned it as blasphemous and demanded it be banned. Mahfouz concurred with the decision of the political leadership to ban the book and anything written about it in order to avoid confrontation. The serialized version was continued, but the book was published in Beirut in 1967. Moreover, Mahfouz was dismissed from his job as head of the Cinema Institute because of the objections of government ministers.75 In 1981, a highly acclaimed English translation by Philip Stewart appeared under the title Children of Gebelawi making the work accessible to a much wider audience. When Mahfouz was awarded the Nobel Prize for literature in 1988, the Swedish Academy speciﬁcally named The Children of Gebelawi alongside the trilogy. Some of Egypt’s leading critics called for al-Azhar to permit publication of the work, and a daily newspaper began serializing it again. At the same time, an Islamist newspaper attacked the novel as

T M W• V 93 • J 2003 130 blasphemous and the author as an apostate. Mahfouz did not participate in the debate and asked that publication of the novel be ceased.76 The furor had hardly died down when later in the year Salman Rushdie published The Satanic Verses, a novel which contained a number of chapters based on material from the life of the Prophet Muhammad.77 Rushdie does not appear to have been inﬂuenced by Mahfouz, but conservative Islamic circles connected the two works, magnifying the perceived danger to Islam and its Prophet. Typically, Mahfouz’s response to the tempest aroused in the West and in the Islamic world was considered. He condemned Khomeini’s death sentence on Rushdie and reafﬁrmed the writer’s freedom of expression as “sacred.” As for his own banned book, Mahfouz reiterated that Egyptian religious authorities did not understand its true meaning, which contained nothing slanderous to Islam and the Prophet. So long as they maintained their opposition, however, he would comply with it.78 Meanwhile, Islamist ideologues took up the attack on Mahfouz and on Awlad Haratina.79 Mahfouz portrays Gabalawi=God as looking toward his harem quarters; the Islamist Shaykh ‘Abd al-Hamid Kishk regards this as the height of sacrilege. One must give the shaykh credit for reading and trying to analyze Mahfouz’s work (even if he does not fathom the principles of the allegory) but some of Kishk’s comments raise doubts about his knowledge of classical Islamic sources. Kassem=Muhammad’s so-called womanizing and multiple marriages are explicitly derived from the classical siras, Qur’anic exegesis and hadith collections. Despite Mahfouz’s growing fame and inﬂuence outside Egypt (or perhaps because of it), the Islamist verbal and physical assaults upon him did not cease. Writers, intellectuals, government ofﬁcials and journalists, in Egypt and abroad, condemned the stabbing of a sick old man. A proposal was made to publish Awlad Haratina under the ofﬁcial government imprimatur. In fact, the weekly al-Ahali, in deﬁance of conservative Muslim sentiment, published the full text of Awlad Haratina in a special supplement, priced at one Egyptian pound an issue, so that it could be widely distributed. The issue sold out very quickly, but was not reprinted.80 Mahfouz’s groundbreaking allegory on the life of Muhammad has a feminist thrust but, as several critics have noted, Mahfouz’s feminism is realistic and incisive rather than didactic. This is no simplistic message of the Prophet Muhammad as the prime advocate of women’s liberation. There are several obstacles to the dissemination of Mahfouz’s subtle feminism. Readers are more impressed by the patriarchal social reality depicted than they are by the low-key, pervasive inﬂuence or the more overt power of women. Also, the audience for such a profound work is limited, and the ban on its publication in Egypt as well as the attacks by the religious

M’ CHILDREN OF GEBELAWI 131 establishment present practical as well as subliminal barriers for potential readers. Ironically, it may well be that more Anglophones, Francophones and Swedes have been exposed to The Children of Gebelawi than Arabic-readers. Nevertheless, Mahfouz’s Islamic allegory took the life of the Prophet to a new literary plane and provided the author with the freedom to use Islamic materials in innovative ways.
